claims.text: Toughness retention or loss in HEAs is governed by the balance between nanoscale grain-boundary second-phase formation and maintenance of a single-phase solid solution.
Increasing the concentration of a refractory or high-melting element such as W or Mo promotes brittle intermetallic precipitation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary precipitation of brittle intermetallic phases reduces toughness relative to a baseline single-phase alloy.
The baseline HEA has a predominantly single-phase solid-solution microstructure and high intrinsic toughness.
Systematically increasing the targeted refractory-element concentration can induce nanoscale second phases.
The relevant structural mediator is the formation and distribution of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries.
Increasing the refractory-element concentration beyond its solubility limit causes brittle intermetallic phases to nucleate at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates act as stress concentrators under mechanical loading.
Grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates serve as crack-initiation sites.
Stress concentration and crack initiation at the precipitates reduce fracture toughness.
Modified alloys with increased refractory-element content will have lower fracture toughness than the baseline single-phase alloy.
Modified alloys will exhibit second-phase precipitates along grain boundaries.
The proposed behavior is limited to alloys in which the refractory-element solubility limit is exceeded without accompanying processing variations.
The proposed behavior applies only over temperatures where thermal activation does not markedly reverse precipitate formation.
The refractory-element concentration threshold for brittle-phase formation depends on the specific HEA composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The design says identical heat treatments will ensure consistent microstructures, whereas the intervention is explicitly intended to create composition-dependent microstructural differences. Identical processing can control processing history but cannot ensure identical microstructures across the composition series.
